terms.grammar: conjunction, with the present indicative, even of past time
evidence: Sen. Ep. 7.8: hominēs, dum docent, discunt
Hor. S. 1.5.71–72: paene … ārsit dum turdōs versat in ignī
terms.comment: The longer action during which something else happens. Latin keeps the present after dum even when the main verb is past: ārsit dum … versat, he caught fire while he was turning. Where the two last equally long, “as long as”, see that record.

evidence: Cic. Tusc. 5.97: Sōcratēn ferunt, cum ūsque ad vesperum contentius ambulāret …
terms.comment: The background against which a past event happens.

terms.grammar: the present participle, agreeing with its noun
evidence: Cic. Sen. 17: ille autem clāvum tenēns quiētus sedeat in puppī
terms.comment: “While holding”, “while walking”: the commonest Latin for an English “while …ing”. Lewis & Short has participium as the grammarians’ word (Varro, Quintilian).

phrases.latin: mūtuō ista fīunt, et hominēs, dum docent, discunt
phrases.english: it works both ways: people learn while they teach

phrases.latin: diēs nihil est. dum versās tē, nox fit
phrases.english: a day is nothing. While you turn round, night falls

phrases.latin: sēdulus hospes paene macrōs ārsit dum turdōs versat in ignī
phrases.english: our busy host nearly caught fire while he was turning the lean thrushes on the fire
while it is put off, life runs past

phrases.latin: Sōcratēn ferunt, cum ūsque ad vesperum contentius ambulāret quaesītumque esset ex eō quārē id faceret, respondisse sē, quō melius cēnāret, obsōnāre ambulandō famem
phrases.english: they say that Socrates, when he was walking hard till evening and was asked why, answered that he was buying in hunger by walking, so as to dine better
